dct_description_sm: The eddy covariance method is a means of observing surface exchanges of energy, momentum, and mass.  It is based on the premise that such exchanges can be calculated from high-frequency three-dimensional velocity measurements of turbulent flow within a fluid, in conjunction with other characteristics of the turbulence (e.g. temperature, mass concentration, etc.).  To date, the application of underwater eddy covariance to sea ice studies has largely focused on three areas: momentum transfer between the sea ice and the ocean, which is a critical component in understanding and modeling ice drift; heat transfer, which is important in understanding the energy balance and growth/melt rates of sea ice; and salt flux, which is important for understanding ice growth and decay, mixed layer stratification, and biogeochemical cycling.  Very recently, the oxygen eddy covariance method has been applied to sea ice for the purpose of measuring under-ice primary production.  This is an exciting development, as the direct measurement of gas exchange under sea ice has the potential to improve understandings of ice-ocean biogeochemical cycles.
dct_title_s: Underwater Eddy Covariance Data in Dease Strait
